proves: OPS-05: on a clean host, the newest published release image, pulled by its pinned tag, is the image that runs: the registry digest, the digest recorded by the release workflow, the pulled image's repo digest, the container's image id, the binary in the running process and the version and commit the portal reports all agree, and the compose file and its image reference are byte-identical before and after the deploy

OPS-06: a recovery set taken with the released build is verified (file digests, secret_key fingerprint, a dry-run restore by that build) before a rollout; after a forced failed rollout the prior build refuses the migrated database; and the restore refuses a bad set before the live stack is touched (a dump written by the newer build, a truncated set and a set with the wrong secret_key each fail their check) and passes the good one in the recorded order: integrity, dry-run compatibility, and a scratch-database rehearsal that signs in a two-factor account whose secret is sealed under the keyring, all before the live database is replaced and the prior version activated

OPS-06: after restore the platform is back on the prior version by digest, the compose reference, secret_key fingerprint, keyring rows, migration ledger and fixture data (users, report, API token) equal their pre-rollout values and the two-factor account signs in
not_proven: No real server, production database, production secret_key or the production deployment procedure's host-level parts (reverse proxy, firewall, systemd ordering, shared PostgreSQL) are involved

The candidate used as the failed rollout is the released image's runtime layers with a binary built from the commit under test and without the web bundle; it is not a release image built by the release workflow

No app runner is on the host: runner/Portal protocol compatibility, the runner journal, managed app data and image blobs are not part of the recovery set exercised here, so the runtime half of 'Portal/runtime compatibility' is covered only as Portal build against database ledger
The recovery set is the existing logical dump plus the config directory; the platform recovery bundle (writePlatformRecoveryBundle) is not reachable from any command and is not used

The failed rollout is one injected fault (config not carried across) on top of the schema step the candidate applies; other failure modes (a build that never starts, an image that cannot be pulled, a failing migration) are not drilled
The deployed release is a pre-release of the beta channel; its content and ledger are the main-branch line, not the platform candidate
known_limits: The cited run is push-triggered on the branch (temporary trigger, reverted); evidence_blockers is empty for push and workflow_dispatch events, and a dispatch repeat after the workflow reaches the default branch should replace this citation

The restore replaces the migrated database by renaming it and restoring into a fresh one, because the prior build refuses to open a database whose ledger it does not know; a restore cannot be applied over the migrated database
The two-factor sign-in is the key-recovery oracle: it proves the keyring opens under the recovered secret_key, not that every sealed secret in a real database would
